title: How vaccines train your immune cells
examples: How does the body remember a germ?

explain.say: Your immune system learns to recognise germs by their shape. A vaccine lets it practise on a harmless version first, so it is ready for the real thing.

explain.say: A vaccine contains a safe lookalike: a weakened or killed germ, a piece of one, or instructions for your cells to make a piece. Immune cells pick it up and show its shape to other immune cells.

stages.label: Fast defence later
stages.note: The real germ is met quickly

explain.say: White blood cells called B cells and T cells that happen to match that shape multiply. B cells make antibodies, Y-shaped proteins that lock onto the germ's shape and mark it for destruction.

explain.say: Some of these cells become memory cells that stay in your body for years. If the real germ arrives, they recognise it and launch a big, fast response before it can spread far.

faq.a: Memory cells are B and T cells that stay in the body after a first meeting with a germ or vaccine. They recognise the same germ later and quickly start a stronger defence.
asks: How does the body remember a germ?

faq.a: Antibodies are Y-shaped proteins made by B cells. Each one fits a particular shape on a germ, like a key in a lock, and helps neutralise it or mark it for other immune cells to destroy.
asks: Tell me about antibodies being made

faq.a: A vaccine contains something that shows the immune system a germ's shape without causing the disease: a weakened or inactivated germ, a harmless piece of it, or genetic instructions like mRNA for cells to make that piece.
asks: Tell me about the harmless lookalike

faq.q: Why is the second meeting with a germ different?
faq.a: The first time, the immune system needs days to find and multiply the right cells. The second time, memory cells are already waiting, so the response is faster and much stronger.
Edward Jenner developed the first vaccine in 1796, using material from cowpox to protect against smallpox. The word vaccine comes from the Latin for cow, vacca.
asks: Where does the word vaccine come from?

facts: Edward Jenner tested the first vaccine, against smallpox, in 1796.
